question: Which of the following is an ABSOLUTE contraindication to corneal donation for transplantation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Age per se is NOT an absolute contraindication. Corneas from donors up to 80 years can be used if the endothelial cell count is adequate (>2,000 cells/mm²). Age is a relative factor requiring specular microscopy evaluation.

answers.text: Death due to rabies or Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rabies, CJD (prion disease), and unknown cause of death are ABSOLUTE contraindications — the risk of transmitting a uniformly fatal neurological disease to the recipient is unacceptable. These are non-negotiable exclusions.

answers.text: History of controlled diabetes mellitus in the donor

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Controlled diabetes is a relative (not absolute) contraindication. The cornea is evaluated by specular microscopy for endothelial cell density. Well-controlled diabetics with adequate cell counts can donate.

answers.text: Donor death more than 8 hours prior to enucleation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The recommended death-to-enucleation time is within 6 hours (ideally), but up to 12 hours is acceptable with proper precautions (closed eyes, refrigerated body). This is a logistic challenge, not an absolute contraindication.

overallFeedback.feedback: Absolute contraindications include rabies, CJD, HIV, active hepatitis B/C, unknown cause of death. Age >70 and diabetes are relative — specular microscopy guides the decision.

Correct! Absolute contraindications = rabies, CJD/prion diseases, unknown cause of death, septicaemia, HIV, hepatitis B/C (active), leukaemia, lymphoma. Age and diabetes are relative — use specular microscopy to decide.
